summary: A 1977 version of the Telnet Data Entry Terminal option, replacing RFC 731. It is updated by RFC 1043.

plainLanguage.summary: The Data Entry Terminal option lets a Telnet host control a terminal screen and its form fields. The two sides first agree on supported features, then exchange commands to position the cursor, format fields and send entered data.

subtitle: Telnet commands for negotiating and controlling a screen-based data entry terminal.

tldr.problem: Basic Telnet was designed for scroll-mode terminals, while data-entry terminals need screen positioning, formatted fields and controlled data transmission.
tldr.mechanism: The Data Entry Terminal option defines Telnet subcommands for negotiating terminal features and for editing, erasing, transmitting and formatting screen content.
tldr.outcome: RFC 732 obsoletes RFC 731 and was updated by RFC 1043. The option's subcommands add overhead, and the RFC describes using the Byte Macro Option to reduce it.

sections.title: A Shared Model for Form Terminals
sections.content:
Telnet was first designed for scroll-mode terminals. This option adds support for data-entry terminals with a keyboard and rectangular display. It defines a Network Virtual Data Entry Terminal (NVDET) so different physical terminals can use a shared set of screen controls.

Terminal controls travel in Telnet subnegotiations rather than using ASCII characters in the data stream. Peripheral devices such as printers are outside this option's scope. The default is that neither side uses the Data Entry Terminal (DET) option.
sections.plainLanguage: The option defines common commands for terminals that display forms. The commands travel separately from the text shown or entered on the screen.

sections.title: Negotiating Terminal Features
sections.content:
The option uses Telnet option code 20. Its four facility subcommands describe editing, erasing, transmitting and formatting features. A facility map tells the other side which functions are available or desired.

Before using a function outside the minimal implementation, a server must request its facility. The two sides determine the available functions by taking the logical intersection of their maps. The minimum implementation includes basic cursor movement, screen erase and transmit, data formatting, error reporting, and the Output Line Width and Output Page Size options.
sections.plainLanguage: The hosts exchange lists of terminal functions. They can use only functions that both sides report as available.

sections.title: Editing, Formatting and Transmitting
sections.content:
Editing subcommands move the cursor, insert or delete characters and lines, and report the cursor position. Erase subcommands clear the screen or selected areas. Transmit subcommands send the whole screen, a line, a field, or selected unprotected or modified fields.

FORMAT DATA applies attributes to the following characters, including blinking, reverse video, justification, intensity and protection. Protection can prevent changes or limit entries to alphabetic or numeric characters. An error subcommand reports problems, while the implementation should still try to carry out the command's intent.

The sample interaction builds a form, protects its labels, allows the user to fill in fields and transmits the unprotected entries. The RFC notes that subnegotiations are longer than many terminal commands and describes optional Byte Macro use to represent a command string with one byte.
sections.plainLanguage: Commands can move the cursor, clear parts of the screen, set rules for fields and send selected entries. The example shows a host preparing a form and receiving the fields that the user can edit.
